The *Tīrthavivecana-kāṇḍa* is the eighth part of Lakṣmīdhara’s great digest (*nibandha*), and it is the second section of that work to be published.
The publication of later divisions of a *nibandha* prior to...
The preceding requires a brief explanation. Through the operation of numerous causes, which can only now be conjectured,
the *Kṛtyakalpataru* has almost entirely vanished, and no complete copy exists anywhere.
A copy of it has come to light. Libraries are fortunate indeed that possess even a portion or two of it in a transcript no more than two centuries old.
In publishing this work, the aim has been to utilize all available manuscripts.
Any section that might be discovered through diligent search.
There are obvious difficulties in basing a book upon a single manuscript, even if its text is reasonably correct. In the case of the...
The *Kṛtyakalpataru*, however, being the product of a scribal tradition (*andhaparamparā*) that transcribed from predecessors lacking superior equipment,
has resulted in texts that are far from satisfactory. In the case...
In the preparation of a tolerable text, some divisions have received valuable assistance from an unexpected source. The *Nibandha* of Lakṣmīdhara was held in such high esteem by later writers that...
They made extensive use of it, some even to the extent of transcribing into the pages of their own books not only passages from earlier *nibandhas*, but entire chapters comprising them.

quotations, reproduced in the same order as in the original, along with comments and verbal interpretations. It may be said with justice that some of the later digests are merely constructed upon a central [framework].
The core provided by Lakṣmīdhara was overlaid with further citations from sources that he himself had rejected; this is evident,
for example, in Caṇḍeśvara’s Gṛhastharatnākara.
In relation to the *Gṛhastha-kāṇḍa* of the *Kṛtya-kalpataru*,
the *Dāna-khaṇḍa* of Hemādri’s *Caturvarga-cintāmaṇi*,
the *Dāna-kalpataru*, and the section on [pilgrimage] in Mitramiśra’s *Tīrthaprakāśa*.

The *Tīrtha* section of the *Kṛtyakalpataru*, now being published; but for this assistance, and the circumstance of the discovery of a manuscript of the *Tīrthakāṇḍa* during a special visit I made to the library...
of the Bhonsle Mahārājas at Nagpur, and the acquisition of another manuscript of it for the Library of the Punjab University by Pandit R. A. Sastri (who brought this fact to my attention).
[[page 4-to-4]] VI.
THE SECTION ON SACRED FORDS (TĪRTHA-KĀṆḌA)
[Note] Its present publication may have been delayed because two manuscripts known to exist in Mithilā were unavailable,
despite efforts to obtain them.

The *Tīrtha* section of the *Kalpataru* possesses certain special claims to our attention. It appears to be the first systematic restatement of the theory of *tīrtha-yātrā* (pilgrimage), which had previously been treated [in earlier works].

It appeared sporadically in epic and Purāṇic literature and was hardly noticed in the legal codes (*dharmaśāstra*). Its inclusion in a *dharmaśāstra*-nibandha was an explicit assertion of its status as...

Pilgrimage is an integral part of the recognized scheme of Hindu life. By what it omitted as much as by what it described, the *Tīrthakalpataru* provided an authoritative decision on every matter upon which [it touched].

The practice, which was presumed to be grounded in the authority of the Purāṇas or the Smṛtis, was thereby justified. Examples of this may be found in the Introduction. Later writers on the subject merely expand upon it.

And some of these points or aspects have been established through scholastic discussions conducted with a display of learning and logic. Such is the enumeration of so many *tīrthas*, and particularly those numbering around three hundred.
[To confine] them within the narrow limits of Benares, whose boundaries are defined by the curve of the Gaṅgā and the confines of the two streams of the Vāraṇā and the Asi, might...
This seems to make Lakṣmīdhara an Indian Pausanias;
yet the Greek was animated only by antiquarian feeling, and not by the pious motive to discover a mode of life in this existence.
This will assist in the struggle that might otherwise endure through countless incarnations, bringing an end to the endless transit "from the womb to the tomb" and back again to the womb.
Unlike the pilgrim-guides and Bædekers or Murrays produced nowadays under administrative encouragement for the manifest economic advantage a country might gain from a developed [tourist industry],...
Tourist traffic aside, Hindu works on *tīrtha* dwelt even more upon the "inner" preparation for the pilgrimage than upon its externalities. A proper understanding of the evolution of...

The theory of *tīrtha* is required to dispel vulgar sorcery by endowing the waters of a sacred ford with a purifying power that transcends the merely physical, regardless of the mental or spiritual state of the individual.
The attitudes of pilgrims, upon which the professional priests at the great Tīrthas and their hangers-on— who lie in wait for pilgrims hundreds of miles away— subsist.
It is this contribution of Lakṣmīdhara and of the treatises modeled upon his that has been the aim of the Introduction (pp. 5–5).

The fruit of a pilgrimage (*tīrtha-phala*) is itself a spiritual preparation that culminates in the ecstasy of attaining the sacred site (*tīrtha*). The raptures of the pilgrim...
Those who, through their arduous journey, cry out "Gangā, Gangā" toward the divine stream,
and who humble themselves at the very first sight of the river or a sacred field such as Kāśī and offer salutations to it— these are the marks of this [devotion].
feeling. It would be erroneous to treat a work on *tīrtha*, such as Lakṣmīdhara’s, either as a mere priestly manual or as a simple pilgrim’s itinerary. The seemingly dry discussions of ritual and...
The gradations of benefit arising from pilgrimage possess a philosophical background that is frequently overlooked. It is noteworthy that,
alongside the practical statesmanship expected of him, [this background persists].
Lakṣmīdhara sets aside certain more stringent rules,
such as those concerning mandatory tonsure and the use of vehicles. Later writers, who were more scholiasts than...
Statesmen delight in discussions of the rituals which he does not emphasize.
An examination of the *tīrtha-vivecanas* preceding and following him reveals the lines of evolution in the Hindu theory of pilgrimage.
This is what the Introduction has attempted to clarify: the connection between fasts, the satisfaction of the *manes*, and the concepts of sin, expiation, and purification.
The mental and physical purity of the pilgrim must be clarified; this has been attempted in the Introduction. The function of a modern editor of such a work is to correct...
The elliptical treatment of the *nibandhas*,
which presupposes an intimate familiarity with the philosophical and religious background of life that is now rare, [highlights] the difference between the ancient Hindu...
And the modern outlook may be most clearly seen in the attitude toward death and suffering. The assumption that the doctrines of *saṃsāra* and *karma* have their roots in a belief in predestination—
The denial of human volition has been exposed in modern studies of Indian philosophy. This is because man is the architect of his own fortune and the master of his destiny; therefore, pilgrimage—
Magical practices are acceptable as means of grace.
For those who believe in the Hindu theory of the survival of the personality and *karma*, death holds no terrors. When one—

The *Tīrtha-kāṇḍa*, which demarcates Bengal from the sacred land of Utkala, sanctified by the presence of the Lord of the World (*Jagannātha*).
His city, Puri, whispers into the ears of the pilgrim the mantra that links the worldly stream with the stream of the other world, after which it is named; and...

which the disembodied souls must cross. It is this spirit that causes the pilgrim to "scorn delights and live laborious days" during the course of the journey, and to maintain this mode of life after his [return].
Return home. It is this very same spirit that even today looks with disapproval upon well-intentioned efforts, for the sake of public health, to discourage or prohibit festivals or gatherings.
Pilgrims at great *tīrthas* and *kṣetras*. When a pilgrim is advised to seek liberation by undertaking the *mahāprasthāna*— the journey from which there is no return— or by finding a shortcut.

Whether he seeks liberation by drowning himself at the confluence of sacred rivers or by leaping from the precipice of Amarakaṇṭaka, what is the point of attempting to save his "life" (and prolong its duration)?
[Why] would he place obstacles in the way of his [attaining liberation from the] suffering of endless rebirth?
Therefore, the provision of facilities for pilgrims was...
Dharma. The Indian roadside is dotted with stands of stone upon which the weary pilgrim may rest his load. It is punctuated with *satrās*, tanks, and wells. The planting of shade-giving...

The planting of trees along the roads was primarily for the benefit of pilgrims. Much like the pilgrim-friar in medieval Europe, the Indian pilgrim has been free to travel across the entire breadth and length of the vast continent.
The lives of Indian saints such as Caitanya and Rāmdās Samarth demonstrate how they wandered without hindrance from shrine to shrine, from *tīrtha* to *tīrtha*. The greatest of the South...
The Indian king Kulottuṅga Coḷa secured enduring fame by abolishing tolls throughout his dominions. His action captured the imagination, and he is remembered as the Coḷa who put an end to them.

While the administrative and economic justification for such a highly beneficial measure may be observed, it is necessary [to consider] its value. [The text continues: "with an odious (and impious) exaction (Suṅgam tavirtta Solan)."
The unimpeded pilgrimage, which it is the duty of the Hindu king to foster, should not be overlooked. Among all the unpopular measures of Muslim rule, the most odious was the tax on...

pilgrims. The monk Kavindrācārya gained renown for securing its suspension from Shah Jahan (see G.O.S., XVII, p. v). Its absence during the period of the East India Company may be counted among [the reasons for its decline].
the attractions of its rule. But for weakening religious senti- [[page 7-to-7]] PREFACE
ixthly, due to the weakening of faith, its successor— the modern pilgrim tax, upon which municipalities in pilgrimage centers thrive— would...
be quite as loathsome.
From the perspective of the historian, the study of *tīrtha* literature possesses many attractions. The history of sacred...
Places such as Kāśī, and the discovery of the dates of its shrines and monuments, are clearly services to history. We can distinguish between ancient and spurious shrines, and between...
Ancient and late works claim equal antiquity and authority; yet, the value of this literature is greater in a respect that is less obvious. Pilgrimage contributed to the unification of India.
culture through the steady circulation of the moral elite within the population of the Indian continent. Kāśī was the lodestone that drew South Indians to Hindusthān. Near Setu...
Rāmeśvaram drew pilgrims from the north to the embankment that Rāma had constructed during the epic conflict to vindicate the honor of a woman. The vast areas that a pilgrim would occupy...
The necessity of traveling through territories ruled by those of a foreign or hostile faith was merely an unpleasant incident that the pilgrim had to encounter.
Whether political ambitions united or divided the country, [the situation remained the same].
Pilgrimage forged a unity rooted in religion and a faith in certain eternal truths. Long before astute statesmanship attempted or achieved the unification of India, Akhaṇḍa...
Hindusthān sprang from the wanderings of pilgrims;
it has been so for the Muslims as well. The Haj, born of the genius of the Prophet, has united the Islamic world, and not—
Caliphate.
From a social standpoint, pilgrimage is noteworthy for its leveling influence. [It disregards] sex, color, civil status, and economic [condition].
Inequality and the traditions of servitude that rendered certain classes untouchable all vanished in the presence of the pilgrimage (tīrtha-yātrā). It was the means for the "salvation of all."
It has been the aim of the editor to draw attention to some of these features, so that the wisdom of Lakṣmīdhara in making this a cardinal section of his survey of Hindu duty may be duly appreciated.
It may be properly appreciated. Tīrtha literature must be read with due regard for its historical and cultural background.

The eighth book of the *Kṛtyakalpataru* is designated by its author as the *Tīrthavivecanakāṇḍa*. This great digest (*nibandha*) is the oldest extant work of its kind and one of the earliest of its genre.
the class. It is also one of the largest as well as the most comprehensive. It aims at being complete and self-contained, viewed as an exposition of current views on Dharma, which...
It would provide guidance for kings to follow its precepts themselves and ensure they were duly observed by their subjects. The voluminous nature of this *nibandha* is due to its...
the scope and the expansion of interpretation by the eleventh century.
Yet, it is not diffuse. What is stated in one *kāṇḍa* is rarely reproduced in another. Lakṣmīdhara aimed for conciseness. "Of authorities..."

"Regarding the same subject matter, a text is presented in one location and another in a different context, as required by its specific purpose," he declares in one of the verses of the introduction to the compendium. What...
That which is founded on correct knowledge is proclaimed, while that which is based on ignorance is rejected even if it is popular; ambiguities are cleared away,
and only that which is accepted by all authoritative sources is upheld.
"has been stated;
and where controversy has been endless, Lakṣmīdhara has given a decision. He assumes that he would be read by...

It is noteworthy that there are scholars who do not require elaborate explanations, and who, from even the briefest indications— or even without them— would know which mantra and *prayoga* to employ in every situation.
Subsequent writers, who attempted to improve upon the *Kalpataru*,
could only add matters that had been omitted— matters which might well have been left to the discretion of the judge or the priest. In Lakṣmīdhara’s day, it was...

(Tīrthapraśna 19) – 3. VII, 15: The [text] states: "In this world, there are four types of persons who are worthy of offerings. What are those four? Therefore, one should give to the one who has performed the Agnihotra. If one gives to someone other than these, it is as if one were giving to a crow. Thus says the Śruti. What is the meaning of this? It means that among these four, the one who has performed the Agnihotra is the most excellent. Why? Because he is the one who has completed his duties. Therefore, one should give to him alone. If one gives to anyone else, it is as if one were giving to a crow, for such a person is not a fit recipient. This is what the Śruti intends to convey. Thus ends the section. Now, regarding the question: "What is the definition of a Brāhmaṇa?"—it is said: "He who knows the Veda is a Brāhmaṇa. Among them, the one who has performed the Agnihotra is the most distinguished. Why? Because he has fulfilled the primary obligation. Therefore, one should give to him. Now, regarding the doubt: "Is it only the one who has performed the Agnihotra who is a fit recipient, or are all four equally fit?"—the answer is: All four are indeed fit recipients, but the one who has performed the Agnihotra is the most excellent among them. Why? Because he has accomplished the highest goal. Therefore, one should prefer him. If one gives to someone other than him, it is as if one were giving to a crow, meaning it yields no spiritual merit. This is the conclusion of the Śruti. Thus it is explained. Now, regarding the further inquiry: "What is the nature of the Veda?"—it is said: "The Veda is that which is revealed by the sages and is free from human authorship. Pāda 2, Udāna 10. *Sāriputtasutta* (The Discourse to Sāriputta) At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then the Venerable Sāriputta approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to the Venerable Sāriputta: “Sāriputta, when a bhikkhu is possessed of five qualities, it is fitting for his fellow monks to attend upon him, and it is fitting for him to attend upon his fellow monks. What five? Here, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest transgressions, and having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. This is the first quality... Furthermore, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu has learned much, remembers what he has heard, and accumulates what he has learned. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life—such teachings he has learned much of, retained in mind, recited verbally, mentally investigated, and penetrated well by view.

This is the second quality... Furthermore, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu is one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. This is the third quality... Furthermore, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu possesses the wisdom that arises from seclusion, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. This is the fourth quality... Furthermore, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu has realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, which are free from clinging, and having attained them, he dwells therein. This is the fifth quality. When a bhikkhu is possessed of these five qualities, it is fitting for his fellow monks to attend upon him, and it is fitting for him to attend upon his fellow monks. 8.5 The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? They are: the person who is like a heap of filth, the person who is like a cesspool, the person who is like a jewel casket, and the person who is like a great ocean. And what, monks, is the person who is like a heap of filth? Here, monks, a certain person is reborn in a noble family—one of the khattiyas, the brahmins, or the householders—and he is handsome, attractive, and possessed of great beauty; he is wealthy, with vast possessions and great wealth. But he is immoral, of bad character, one who destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehood, and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence. This, monks, is called the person who is like a heap of filth. “And what, monks, is the person who is like a cesspool? Here, monks, a certain person is reborn in a noble family—one of the khattiyas, the brahmins, or the householders—and he is handsome, attractive, and possessed of great beauty; he is wealthy, with vast possessions and great wealth. He is virtuous, of good character, abstaining from the destruction of life, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence. Yet he does not possess the virtues that are untorn, unrent, unblemished, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, unadulterated, and conducive to concentration. This, monks, is called the person who is like a cesspool. “And what, monks, is the person who is like a jewel casket? Here, monks, a certain person is reborn in a humble family—one of the carters, bamboo-workers, or waste-removers—and he is ugly, unattractive, and lacking in beauty; he is poor, with meager possessions and little wealth. But he is virtuous, of good character, abstaining from the destruction of life, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence. He possesses the virtues that are untorn, unrent, unblemished, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, unadulterated, and conducive to concentration. This, monks, is called the person who is like a jewel casket. “And what, monks, is the person who is like a great ocean? Here, monks, a certain person is reborn in a noble family—one of the khattiyas, the brahmins, or the householders—and he is handsome, attractive, and possessed of great beauty; he is wealthy, with vast possessions and great wealth. this fruit for every morsel of food has indeed been proclaimed according to the rule;

He who, filled with faith, gives food and other offerings to the deities, shall eat for a hundred thousand years together with the immortals, even from every single grain of rice.
Ten times this merit is obtained from a pure vessel endowed with the proper syllables;
this merit is proclaimed as being equal to that given by one's chosen deity.
Whoever bestows food obtains double the fruit;
therefore, by giving food to Viṣṇu, one enjoys double the fruit.
By the offering of food to Rudra, this fruit is fourfold,
due to the conjunction of faith and the proper time, and through the inclusion of various side dishes.

far removed is the talk of knowledge. Nevertheless, the gift that purifies from sin awakens for the life-force of the world—so says the virtuous Śrīmitra Miśra.

One who is overcome by the aforementioned [faults] and touched by defects is not desired [as a teacher]. The partial transgression of the Veda is [remedied] by the imperishable [recitation] of even a slightly deficient portion. "Nibhṛta" means tranquil. "Laukika" refers to knowledge acquired through wealth and so forth. "Nivṛta" means free from prohibited and desire-driven actions. "Niṣkriya" means devoid of activities such as the acquisition of wealth.

In sacrifices and other such rites, when one is overcome— that is, surpassed— by those previously mentioned people who are deficient in knowledge and conduct due to faults such as minor offenses (*upapātaka*), Vasiṣṭha says:
"That which is neither a sacrificial session (*satra*) nor a non-sacrificial session, neither learned nor widely learned..."
No one, including a Brāhmaṇa, knows whether another is of good conduct or of bad conduct.

The intended meaning is that he who belongs to the lineage of Vasiṣṭha, who has abandoned the conduct of the wicked, and who does not openly manifest self-deprecation here, is a worthy recipient (*pātra*). Yama and Śātātapa state:
"Austerity, the dawning of righteousness, truthfulness, purity, knowledge, compassion, and mercy [are the qualities of such a person]."
Knowledge, discipline, and non-stealing—this is the defining characteristic of a Brahmin.
2388 Vasiṣṭha
Yoga, austerity, compassion, charity, truthfulness, purity, mercy, self-restraint, learning, specialized knowledge, and faith— this is the defining characteristic of a Brāhmaṇa.
Paiṭhīnasi says:
Forgiveness, self-restraint, compassion, charity, righteousness, truthfulness, sacred learning, and pity— these are [the qualities of dharma].
Knowledge, discernment, and faith—this is the defining characteristic of a Brāhmaṇa.
Some, however, say that knowledge, austerity, truth,
as well as charity, sacred learning, and yoga— this is the characteristic of a Brāhmaṇa.
He who is devoid of both knowledge and austerity is merely a Brahmin by birth; some among men are wise, while others are ignorant, yet they are all called "Brahmins" because of their lineage.
In the second verse, Manu and Vasiṣṭha regard Yama as the supreme deity:
"Those who are not learned in the Vedas, who do not maintain the sacred fires, and who follow the dharma of Śūdras, are not worthy of the Vedic word; regarding this, men cite the following verse."
One who kills his mother is not a brahmin;
nor is one who is a merchant, a performer, one who serves śūdras, a thief, or a physician.
The king should punish that village where twice-born men wander for alms without observing vows or studying the Vedas; for such a village provides sustenance to thieves.
Regarding those who are declared to be non-Brāhmaṇas, the sage Śātātapa said:
"The first among them follows the conduct of a king; the second is a buyer and seller."
The third is the slayer of combatants and so forth; the fourth is the village priest;
and the fifth is the hired servant of those [villages], whether of a village or a city.

But a twice-born man should not worship the eastern direction before sunrise, nor the western direction after sunset; the meaning is that for one of little learning the reward is small, while for one of great learning it is great.

Having severed the heads of enemy kings and secured for the King of Kāśī the earth girt by the ocean,
he has erected this divine tree (the work known as the *Kalpadruma*).
The tree of the Dharma, whose roots are the Vedas, whose trunk is the Smṛtis, whose branches are the Purāṇas, and which is formidable with the long stalks of numerous Prakarana treatises, has spread—
With leaves consisting of scriptural citations, fluttering with the beautiful blossoms of pure knowledge, and yielding the fruits of Dharma, Artha, Kāma, and Mokṣa (Amita).
Now extracting passages from the Purāṇas and now again from the Smṛtis, thus did Gopāla, the friend of Lakṣmīdhara, make his work a mere compilation.
But this concise work shall be performed,
free from any flaw for censure, satisfying the minds of the learned through the essence of the Vedas.
